issues.subcategory: core construct definition mismatch between sections
issues.description: The entire paper defines moral incongruence as the interaction (product) of moral disapproval and behavioral FREQUENCY. However, the 'Present Study' section redefines it as the interaction of moral disapproval with SEVERITY OF CONSEQUENCES. These are fundamentally different operationalizations. The former captures how often someone engages in a disapproved behavior; the latter captures harm experienced. Using consequences as the frequency proxy would actually conflate the predictor (moral incongruence) with the outcome (problematic use consequences), making the entire moderation framework logically circular.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.

issues.subcategory: BPS response scale values inconsistent with stated scoring
issues.description: The methods section describes the Brief Pornography Screen as using 'a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often)' with responses summed. However, the supplemental survey materials show actual response values of Never=0, Occasionally=2, Very Often=4. The implied coding in the text (0, 1, 2) does not match the actual survey coding (0, 2, 4). Using the 0/2/4 values doubles the effective range (max = 20 vs. max = 10) and departs from the validated BPS scoring in Kraus et al. (2020), invalidating comparisons to published norms and cut-scores. The text description of '0 (never) to 2 (very often)' is simply wrong given the supplement.
issues.quote: Participants will respond to the prompt, 'In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you in regards to your use of pornography?' by reporting the frequency they have experienced certain behaviors...on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.subcategory: PGSI response scale, values, and scoring all inconsistent with validated instrument
issues.description: The methods describe the PGSI as using 'a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always)' with responses averaged. The supplemental materials reveal the actual response values are Never=0, Sometimes=2, Most of the time=4, Almost Always=5. Three distinct errors are present: (1) The scale values (0, 2, 4, 5) are entirely non-standard — the validated PGSI uses 0, 1, 2, 3; (2) The irregular spacing (gap between 4 and 5 is 1, not 2 like the prior gaps) suggests a data entry error in the survey instrument; (3) The standard PGSI uses a SUM score with validated clinical cut-points (0=non-problem, 1-2=low risk, 3-7=moderate, 8+=problem gambling). Using an average instead of a sum renders established cut-points meaningless and prevents comparison to the existing clinical literature. The combination of non-standard values and averaging makes this a fundamentally different measure than the validated PGSI.
issues.quote: problem gambling behavior will be measured using the Problem Gambling Severity Index (Ferris & Wynne, 2001). This 9-item measure requires participants to respond to a series of questions...on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.

issues.subcategory: direct contradiction about who completes problematic-use measures
issues.description: The ASSIST substance section explicitly states that only past-year users will complete further problematic use measures: 'Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use.' However, the Data Screening section directly contradicts this: 'For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior.' These two statements are mutually exclusive. The choice between them has major implications for sample sizes, floor effects on problematic use scores (non-users scoring zero), and the validity of interaction models, yet no resolution is provided.
issues.quote: Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use. [...] For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior.

issues.subcategory: internally inconsistent Cohen's d conversion for the same reported effect
issues.description: The same prior-study effect (ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016) is reported with two different Cohen's d values within the same paragraph. In the first listing it is reported as 'Cohen's d = .22' and in the second listing for the identical ΔR2 and f2 values it is described as 'Cohen's d = .25.' This matters because the paper uses this effect to set the SESOI (δ = |.11|), so an error here directly affects the equivalence bounds. Using the approximate conversion d ≈ 2√f2 yields d ≈ 0.253, suggesting the value of .22 is the error. This inconsistency undermines confidence in the SESOI derivation.
issues.quote: ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020 [...] β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .25, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020

issues.subcategory: frequency scale anchor mismatch between methods text and survey instrument
issues.description: The methods section repeatedly describes pornography and gambling frequency scales as running from '1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).' The actual supplemental survey instruments show these scales running from 0 (Never) to 5 (More than Once Per Day). This off-by-one error is consistent across multiple scale descriptions. Because the analysis plan specifies centering and creating interaction terms from these scores, using the wrong scale anchors in the code could introduce systematic errors in all interaction terms, which are the primary statistical test of the key hypotheses.
issues.quote: Pornography viewing frequency will be assessed using the same modified frequency scale as is present on the ASSIST, wherein participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day).

issues.subcategory: gambling frequency operationalized as average of multiple behaviors but only one item exists
issues.description: The methods state 'To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken,' implying multiple gambling frequency items. However, the supplemental survey materials contain only a single gambling frequency item ('Gambled or placed bets at all'). You cannot take an average of multiple items when only one item exists. This discrepancy suggests either a survey design error (planned items were omitted) or a methods-writing error. Either way, the actual gambling frequency measure will be a single item, which has implications for reliability and for how frequency is entered into the moderation model.
issues.quote: To form a measure of gambling frequency, an average across gambling behaviors will be taken.

issues.subcategory: sports-wagering oversample systematically biases gambling analyses
issues.description: The sample includes 2,500 nationally representative U.S. adults plus 1,500 sports-wagering individuals. For gambling analyses, these groups will be combined (effective N = 3,325 gamblers per Table 2). Sports bettors are a highly self-selected subgroup with potentially higher gambling frequency, lower moral disapproval of gambling, and a distinctive relationship between use and problem symptoms compared to casual or lottery-only gamblers. The paper provides no pre-specified weighting strategy, subgroup analysis plan, or sensitivity analysis comparing gamblers-only from the representative sample to the oversample. This compositional confound will distort all gambling moral incongruence estimates, which are central to the primary null hypothesis test (Hypothesis 2b).
issues.quote: we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically. This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: unvalidated NIDA-ASSIST modifications used as primary addiction outcomes
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that including pornography and gambling in the NIDA-ASSIST 'is not currently validated for gambling or pornography.' Despite this, the modified ASSIST items are used as primary outcome measures (and as the sole outcomes for all substances). For the primary test of whether moral incongruence is unique to pornography, the pornography ASSIST items are used alongside the validated BPS. If the unvalidated ASSIST pornography items behave differently from the BPS, it creates ambiguity in interpretation. More critically, for all substance outcomes (the primary null-hypothesis conditions), only the unvalidated ASSIST items are used, meaning the primary evidence for the null effects rests on psychometrically uncharacterized measures.
issues.quote: Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.subcategory: temporal reference windows inconsistent across outcome measures
issues.description: The outcome measures use three different and incompatible reference periods: NIDA-ASSIST problematic use items ask about 'the past three months'; the Brief Pornography Screen asks about 'the last 6 months'; frequency measures and the PGSI ask about 'the past 12 months.' Comparing the strength of moral incongruence effects across behaviors — which is the central purpose of the study — requires that outcomes be measured on comparable scales and time frames. A 3-month assessment window for substances but a 6-month window for pornography means that any differences in observed moral incongruence effects could reflect temporal artifacts rather than behavioral specificity. This inconsistency is never acknowledged or addressed.
issues.quote: In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you in regards to your use of pornography? [...] In the past three months, how often have you had a strong desire or urge to use or engage in the following? [...] Thinking about the last 12 months…

issues.subcategory: no pre-specified correction for multiple simultaneous hypothesis tests
issues.description: The study conducts eight simultaneous moderation analyses (pornography, gambling, alcohol, tobacco/nicotine, cannabis, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, plus a second pornography model) testing correlated hypotheses. No familywise or false-discovery-rate correction is pre-specified for the confirmatory tests. Because the central claim is that moral incongruence is significant for pornography but not for other behaviors, the Type I error rate for the pornography interaction (the one expected to be significant) is inflated by conducting it alongside seven other tests without correction. The decision to apply equivalence testing to non-pornography outcomes and traditional NHST to the pornography outcome is asymmetric and not fully justified as a single coherent inferential framework.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest

issues.subcategory: confirmatory framing incompatible with scientific hypothesis testing
issues.description: Throughout the paper, the stated goal is explicitly to 'demonstrate' a specific outcome — that moral incongruence is unique to sexual behavior — rather than to test whether this is the case. This framing reveals motivated reasoning that is scientifically inappropriate and particularly problematic for a Registered Report, whose purpose is to commit to an unbiased test of hypotheses before data collection. A researcher who aims to 'demonstrate' a result has a directional bias that could influence undisclosed analytic choices. The framing also misrepresents the scientific enterprise: if one already knows the answer, the study's epistemic value is diminished.
issues.quote: Ultimately, we aim to demonstrate that—consistent with the ICD-11 decision to include moral distress as a diagnostic consideration when applying a diagnosis of CSBD—the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior, in contrast with other addictions.

issues.subcategory: SESOI selected from range of effects using post-hoc justification
issues.description: The paper reviews prior moral incongruence effects ranging from f2 = .016 to f2 = .23 — a 14-fold range — and then selects the smallest as the SESOI. The authors frame this as 'extremely conservative,' but selecting the smallest available effect from a heterogeneous set of prior studies to define the equivalence bound is a form of analytic flexibility: a different SESOI choice would change the conclusions. Furthermore, the SESOI is derived from an effect using religiousness (not direct moral disapproval) and a different outcome measure (CPUI-4, not BPS), while the paper simultaneously acknowledges that the BPS-based effect from the most parallel design is β = .27 — nearly 2.5 times the selected SESOI. The post-hoc justification narrative ('extremely conservative analytic decision') does not resolve this flexibility concern.
issues.quote: we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .25, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020). Notably, this effect was observed for an interaction between religiousness (as opposed to moral disapproval directly) and pornography viewing frequency...Additionally, this past work used a different and less rigorously validated outcome measure

issues.subcategory: causal language used throughout cross-sectional study
issues.description: Despite the cross-sectional design (explicitly noted in limitations), the manuscript repeatedly uses causal language — 'moral incongruence is a clear contributor,' 'moral incongruence predicts,' 'moral disapproval amplifies the links.' A cross-sectional moderation analysis cannot establish temporal precedence or rule out reverse causation (e.g., feeling addicted to pornography could increase moral disapproval) or bidirectional effects. The concern is heightened because the independent variable (moral disapproval) and the dependent variable (perceived addiction) are both self-reported attitudes/perceptions collected simultaneously, making common-method bias a plausible confound that could artificially inflate the pornography interaction while not inflating substance use interactions (where disapproval and perceived addiction may be psychologically more independent).
issues.quote: moral incongruence is a clear contributor to self-reported feelings of addiction to, compulsivity in, or problems with pornography use. More simply, moral incongruence predicts feeling out of control in one's pornography use.

issues.subcategory: SESOI derived from pornography-specific effects applied across dissimilar instruments
issues.description: The equivalence bound (δ = |.11| standardized β) was derived from studies using pornography-specific outcomes (CPUI-4 or BPS) with pornography-specific predictors (moral disapproval and frequency of pornography use). This SESOI is then applied to detect whether gambling and substance outcomes — measured with entirely different instruments (PGSI, modified ASSIST) having different psychometric properties, distributions, and response ranges — produce effects that fall within the same equivalence region. The standardized β for an interaction is sensitive to the variance of the outcome variable; instruments with different reliability and variance will yield different effect size estimates for the same true effect, making a cross-instrument SESOI comparison fundamentally problematic without demonstrating scale equivalence.
issues.quote: Should the confidence interval for the observed standardized effect of the interaction for moral disapproval of a behavior and frequency of that behavior fall fully within our equivalence region, we may reasonably conclude that the true effect is so low as to be null or practically null, thereby supporting hypotheses 2b and 3b

issues.subcategory: moral incongruence operationalization conflates non-users who disapprove with users who disapprove
issues.description: Moral incongruence, by definition, requires that a person both engage in a behavior AND disapprove of it. The interaction term (moral disapproval × frequency) applied to the full sample assigns non-zero moral incongruence scores to individuals who disapprove of a behavior they have never engaged in (i.e., disapproval × near-zero frequency). These individuals are not morally incongruent — they are consistent in values and behavior. Including them in the interaction inflates variance in the disapproval predictor without adding valid moral incongruence variance, potentially attenuating the interaction effect. This is particularly relevant for substances with low base rates (prescription drug misuse, illicit drugs) where the majority of the sample are non-users.
issues.quote: moral incongruence is better conceptualized as the interaction of moral disapproval and use, rather than simply as the presence of moral disapproval among users (Grubbs, 2020; Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020; Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020). In this revised definition, use frequency moderates links between moral disapproval and self-reported feelings of addiction

issues.subcategory: pre-registration details absent
issues.description: This is described as a Registered Report, but the manuscript provides no details about where the protocol was registered (e.g., OSF, AsPredicted, ClinicalTrials.gov), the registration date, the registration ID/URL, or what version of the protocol was submitted for Stage 1 review. Without this information, readers cannot verify that the pre-specified hypotheses, analytic plan, and SESOI were not modified after data collection began or after preliminary data were observed. For a Registered Report, this is essential provenance information.
issues.quote: Moral Incongruence and Addiction: A Registered Report

issues.subcategory: men's binge-drinking item label contradicts question stem
issues.description: The survey instrument for men's heavy alcohol use asks 'how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion?' but the response row is labeled 'More than four drinks (1).' The label should read 'More than five drinks.' This discrepancy means that either the question text or the item label will cause participant confusion, potentially leading to systematic measurement error in the alcohol frequency variable, which is one of the primary predictors and outcome measures in this study.
issues.quote: IF GENDER = MAN: In the past year, how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion? [response row label:] More than four drinks (1)

issues.subcategory: severely underpowered subgroups for primary equivalence tests
issues.description: Table 2 shows that the prescription drug misuse subsample (estimated n ≈ 140, 3.5% prevalence) has an estimated achieved power of only .301 for the primary SESOI of f2 = .015. The illicit drug subsample (n ≈ 240–480) achieves power of only .472–.764. Since these subgroups are the focus of primary null hypotheses (Hypothesis 3b), the study lacks the power to either detect an effect at the SESOI threshold or to declare equivalence with confidence at that threshold. While the authors acknowledge this and propose an alternative larger equivalence interval, this adaptive fallback uses a different SESOI from a different prior study, meaning these two null hypotheses are tested using categorically different evidentiary standards from the pornography hypothesis.
issues.quote: However, in the case of illicit drug use (prevalence estimated at 6%-12% of the population) and prescription drug misuse (prevalence estimated at 3.5% of the population), it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required to detect effects that small

issues.subcategory: U.S.-only sample with broad claims about addictions universally
issues.description: The paper's introduction and conclusions make broad claims about the role of moral incongruence 'in the full spectrum of addictions, both substance and behavioral' and about generalizing findings to CSBD diagnosis globally. However, the sample is restricted to U.S. adults. Moral attitudes toward pornography, gambling, alcohol, and drug use vary enormously across cultures, religions, and legal regimes. The prior literature cited (Polish and Croatian samples) found cultural variation in moral incongruence effects. A U.S.-only sample with a Protestant-dominant religious landscape cannot serve as evidence for or against the universality of moral incongruence across addictions, yet the discussion will likely be framed in universal terms.
issues.quote: Should results confirm the above hypotheses, this work would have broad implications for current controversies regarding CSBD...there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD

issues.subcategory: recruitment timing during peak sports-betting season
issues.description: Data collection is scheduled for 'late March of 2022.' In the United States, late March corresponds to the NCAA Men's Basketball Tournament (March Madness), which is the highest-volume annual sports-betting event. Collecting sports-wagering data during this period will systematically elevate betting frequency, emotional engagement with gambling, and potentially problem gambling symptom reports compared to other times of year. This introduces a seasonal confound that will affect the gambling moral incongruence interaction specifically, since betting frequency — the moderator — will be artificially inflated for a large portion of the sports-wagering oversample.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited in late March of 2022 as a part of a larger study of sports wagering behaviors in the American populace

issues.subcategory: pornography frequency restricted to solo use only, departing from prior literature
issues.description: The pornography frequency item asks only about pornography 'viewed alone (i.e., without a partner).' Prior studies in this literature, including those used to derive the SESOI, typically measure pornography viewing frequency without restricting to solo use. Partner pornography use is associated with a distinct psychological profile and different relationships to moral disapproval (which is often rooted in relational ethics). Excluding partner pornography use from the frequency predictor means this study's operationalization of pornography frequency is not directly comparable to the prior studies that generated the effect sizes used for power analysis and SESOI derivation.
issues.quote: Viewed pornography alone (i.e., without a partner)

issues.subcategory: religiousness standardization procedure is non-standard and potentially distorting
issues.description: The analytic plan describes standardizing each religiousness item individually (using what reference distribution is unclear — the full sample, or subsamples?), then averaging the standardized scores, then multiplying by -1. Standard practice is to reverse-code items before aggregating, then standardize the composite if needed. The described procedure will yield a composite that is already in standard deviation units (approximately) before the sign reversal, but individual-item standardization inflates the relative weight of items with smaller SDs (e.g., prayer frequency, which is more variable). The unusual approach is not justified by citation and could produce different results from standard approaches.
issues.quote: upon taking the average of standardized responses to the above three questions, the average will be transformed by multiplying by -1 so that higher scores correspond to higher religiousness.

issues.subcategory: no description of how combined national and oversample will be analyzed or weighted
issues.description: The study combines a nationally representative sample (n=2,500) with a purposive sports-wagering oversample (n=1,500). For analyses involving variables other than gambling (e.g., pornography use, substance use), it is unclear whether the oversample will be included, excluded, or downweighted. Including sports bettors in pornography or substance use analyses inflates sample size but introduces sampling bias since sports bettors are not drawn from a probability sample. The analytic plan does not describe any sample weighting, post-stratification, or sensitivity analysis comparing conclusions with and without the oversample across non-gambling outcomes.
issues.quote: we propose making use of an upcoming, nationally representative study of addictions in the U.S. population...we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports
